Herod the Great. King of Judea from 37 to 4 BCE, ruling with Roman backing during the time of Jesus's birth and early ministry. Though he was effective at maintaining peace and order, Herod is remembered in Christian tradition primarily through the Gospel account of the Massacre of the Innocents—his alleged order to kill all male infants in Bethlehem to prevent the birth of a rival king prophesied by magi.

Herod was not ethnically Jewish but an Idumean whose family converted to Judaism, and he gained power through Roman military support during the civil wars of the late republic. He ruled for thirty-four years, maintaining relative peace and prosperity through ruthless suppression of rebellion and internal political intrigue. He undertook massive building projects, most famously the reconstruction of the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem, making it one of the ancient world's architectural marvels.

He was known for paranoia and cruelty, executing his own sons and wife on suspicion of disloyalty, contributing to the negative portrait in Christian tradition. After Herod's death, his kingdom was divided among his sons, while Judea proper came under direct Roman procuratorial rule, including that of Pontius Pilate. Herod's role as the backdrop to Jesus's infancy, his connection to John the Baptist through his son Herod Antipas, and his monumental construction of the Temple in Jerusalem all ensured his lasting place in the religious consciousness of the Western world.
